utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours much. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. I welcome everyone in the courtroom, Mr. Ferrara, Mr. Mundis and their case manager, their assistants as well, Mr. Seselj, and everyone helping us, notably our Registrar. We will now continue with the cross-examination of the witness. Let me ask our usher to please escort the witness into the courtroom. And could the Registrar please tell me every 30 minutes how far we've been so that I can keep track of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time do I have left, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I wanted to ask our Registrar. I believe that you have an hour and 55 minutes left. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I hope there will be no objections or procedural incidents so that we can finish on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope you had a good night's rest. You may sit down, and I will give the floor to Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before the cross-examination starts, I would have a request, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask Your Honours that in the future, this session be closed for the public, for three reasons. One reason is that my family is afraid. The second reason is I wouldn't like to allow the accused to promote his political party in this way. And, thirdly, due to reasons concerning my privacy. Yesterday, when you asked me whether I trusted this Court, I said, "Yes." Unfortunately, yesterday I felt unprotected on the basis of certain questions that have nothing to do whatsoever with these proceedings and that have to do with my very own privacy. That is one of the reasons why, if I'm not protected from such questions today, I will have to resort to my own mode of protection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're telling me that your family is afraid, but what is your family afraid of? You called them yesterday on the phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't speak to them over the telephone, Your Honour. We exchanged text messages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did they say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I got a message from my daughter, saying that she is afraid. She watched the public broadcast. Everything was out there in the public. And as I departed on this journey, my family had been informed that I would be a protected witness rather than a witness testifying in public, and that's why they're afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, when you came here, you did not tell Mr. Ferrara that you wanted to be granted protective measures. You testified openly and freely. You didn't ask for anything. Now, what we can do, and Mr. Seselj was never opposed to this up until now, anyway, is the following: If he's asking questions on your family or on very specific problems, then we can move into private session. His cross-examination focuses on two essential points, and maybe that's what you can't really understand. First, it's your credibility, to make sure that you're a credible witness, so he is allowed and entitled to ask questions to you to check your credibility. That's the procedure in this Tribunal. It's different in your country, it's different in my country also, but this is the way the procedure has been organised here. The Defence is entitled to test your credibility, and in order to do this, it may delve into your past. And, secondly, the witness is supposed to answer all questions put by the Defence regarding the facts that are in the indictment and regarding the events that occurred in your own village, which is why he has to deal with all these issues. Then, thirdly, it turns out that you are a member of a political party and he's the leader of another political party, and obviously both your parties don't see eye to eye, so that's a problem. So you may say that he's promoting his party. I don't think he needs this. And what you are saying may backfire on you, because you could also try and promote your own party. The Trial Chamber is going to keep a close eye on this. If we think this is turning into a political platform, we'll do something, move into private session or something. But if Mr. Seselj is really delving into very private matters at one point in time or intimate matters, we will move into private session. Does this reassure you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What suits me is closed session. However, if this is your ruling, then I have to reconcile myself to that. Allow me to make yet another observation with regard to these questions. Yesterday, he asked me whether I had ever been in any kind of conflict with a Croat. I said, no, that I did not remember. Then he said that that was not true, that I had beat up a Croat. This is the first time I ever found out that that man was an ethnic Croat, which is to say that this kind of question was planted on me from my past, over 20 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, but when the Defence found out that you were a Prosecution witness, but you could have been a Defence witness, but when they found out you were a Prosecution did witness, they scrutinised your entire past. They checked whether you had ever been convicted. They noted that there was a judgement rendered against you. They checked what it was, and then they saw that there was some kind of fight that you'd forgotten about. And of course the Defence is highlighting all this in order to indicate that this actually happened, that at one point in time you were in conflict with a Croat. But in the end, it's up to the Bench to decide what importance it will give to this matter. That's the way it is now. Maybe in your own country, you know, the judge that would have been asking questions would not have delved into this, but this is different here. The Defence is entitled to control its cross-examination. We're just here to check that you're not being harassed or threatened. Now, we can't go much further than that. If there was a judgement because you -- and you were convicted because of assault, I mean, what can we do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My fellow Judge would like to ask you an additional question. You said that you obtained SMSs, text messages, but did they tell you that you had been threatened since then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My daughter sent me an SMS, a text message, saying that she was surprised and very much afraid, that someone had also phoned my wife. She did not write to me in great detail about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And she called your wife what for? What did she say? You don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm absolutely opposed to moving into closed session, because the entire examination-in-chief was in open session, and I have already completed one-third of my cross-examination in open session. Yesterday, I didn't try and I don't have any intention of mentioning the witness's family. I'm full of respect for his wife, his daughter. I think he has a son as well. I absolutely have no reason to mention their names here. They are not any prominent political figures, so it wouldn't be important to mention their names. I did not ask anything yesterday that infringes upon the witness's privacy. Everything I asked him is a public matter and speaks about his public activity. Sometimes he was held accountable by the law because of his public activity, and sometimes he tried to conceal certain things, as you saw yesterday. However, nothing can be hidden from me. Anyway, there is no reason whatsoever to move into closed session, and there is no threat for his family. I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber has noted your request and has heard Mr. Seselj. We have decided to continue in open session. However, if the Trial Chamber notes that private matters are being discussed at one point in time, we will ask for a private session. We're following this extremely carefully to make sure that we don't run into any problems. We do note that the accused said that he would not address any issues having to do with your family. Furthermore, Mr. Seselj, if at one point in time you need to look into family matters, please ask us, with advanced notice, to move into private session. This being said, Mr. Seselj, you have the floor. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I guarantee to you that I will not go into the domain of the witness's privacy at all. There is no reason for that. I just want to discuss what pertains to his testimony, and that only, his statements made to The Hague investigators and what he said during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Ejic, could you agree with me that refugees from the Croatian federal unit arrived in about three waves in Serbia; the first one was immediately after Tudjman came to power, that is to say, in the second half of 1990 and 1991; the second wave came after the fall of a large part of Western Slavonia in December 1991, when Western Slavonia practically became reduced to the area of Pakrac or, rather, Okucani and this belt area leading to Pakrac, up into the outskirts of Pakrac. And the third wave was in 1995, after Operations Flash and Storm. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that there were several influxes of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: These first arrivals in the first stage were individual or in smaller groups, for the most part; isn't that right? When Tudjman came to power, then the first incidents in Croatia, and then up until the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The second wave was already a massive one in December 1992, because there was a massive exodus of the Serb people from Western Slavonia; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the third even more massive exodus was after Operations Flash and Storm in 1995, when all the western parts of the Serb Krajina were occupied and when the population was expelled; am I not right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my village is concerned, I don't know whether that was the wave, but that there were waves after these operations, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm putting questions that are a bit leading, but I'd like to get answers as fast as possible. Do you believe me that that's the only reason? I have no other trap questions for you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have much trust in you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I know that you have no trust in me, but I have no trust in you, either.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when you falsely accuse me in your books, then of course I don't trust you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. You can respond by writing your own book. You're a literate man, after all, so you can respond in that way if you found anything there that doesn't correspond to the truth. I had the impression, from your answers provided during the examination-in-chief and also some answers provided during my cross-examination, that you represented Hrtkovci as some kind of a central location relating to the influx of Serb refugees from the area of Croatia and the Serb Krajina. Is that actually what you wanted to say, that Hrtkovci was chosen as some kind of centre where these refugees would come in?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I came here to tell the truth, what it was that happened in Hrtkovci. As for the area beyond that, I don't have complete information. My information is incomplete, so I don't wish to speak about that. I don't want to talk about things I don't know exactly. What I know about is Hrtkovci, and that's why I came, so that the public would find out the entire truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. To your estimate, what is the total number of Serb refugees that arrived in Hrtkovci to this day; what would be the approximate number?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, over 1.500, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did they all remain to live in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many stayed on?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the number that entered into an exchange and two settlements that were built as refugee places, and I worked for one of them, so in my estimation, about 1.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The 500, they came, tried to exchange their property, didn't succeed, and went somewhere else to try and do it somewhere else; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly they went to towns. Now, whether they managed to buy any property or exchange any property or were given accommodation in some refugee centres, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that in Serbia, a lot of refugees still live in collective accommodation?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that from television and what the public -- what the media says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So these are people who still haven't got a roof over their heads and haven't been supplied that by the government, and haven't got their own property in order to buy something themselves, and do you know that among those people there are many who, in Croatia, destroyed their properties, placed mines there, devastated the apartments?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of stories like that, but I don't know of any cases myself. I can only rely on what I heard and the stories I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, if at the beginning of 1992, according to official data, there were about 200.000 refugees from different areas of Croatia in Serbia, then is that figure of 1.000 refugees in Hrtkovci just half a per cent out of the total number of refugees in Serbia? That would be the case, wouldn't it, 1.000 compared to 200.000? 0.5 per cent would be the figure.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what math says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That means in Hrtkovci, a negligible number of refugees turned up in relation to the large number of people who came to Serbia, this wave of refugees in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not at the beginning, but later on it would appear that it is as you have just put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I know that your suffering in Hrtkovci was the greatest because you had a lot of problems. A vast number of people arrived. They had to be put up. You didn't have anywhere to put them up. You had to feed them, no food, so that was an objective problem; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But these refugees were frustrated when they came in, frustrated by what they had experienced in life?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, and I feel deeply for those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They lost everything they had, they lost their property, they came in angry, frustrated, having suffered a great deal; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Many of those refugees, especially after the fall of Western Slavonia in December 1991, came on, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, those who came in from Croatian towns previously didn't have weapons; do you agree with that, that first lot that came in 1990 and the first half of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, did you notice anybody bearing weapons? No, okay, I'll leave that. Now, do you know of cases whereby the police found whole arsenals of weapons stashed with individuals of refugees; for example, half a tractor-trailer full of weapons? Were there cases like that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but the -- there was information about that in the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I have police data in the book that you didn't like, but never mind. We're not going to deal with that now. There is information whereby the police seized large quantities of weapons at the homes of some individuals, which were probably intended for the black market in Serbia. You say you heard something about that, but know nothing specific?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Whenever you say you don't know, I'll move on, I won't dwell on that. Now, the next question: Do you know that the whole of Yugoslavia in 1991, 1992, under conditions of a civil war, was faced with a legal system or had a legal system where there were no serious regulations for criminal proceedings against people who had weapons? Do you remember a situation like that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not versed in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, do you know that if somebody illegally was in possession of a pistol and the police uncovers that pistol, all that could be done was he could be had up for a misdemeanor, or would have to pay a fine, or two months in prison, and the greatest sentence would be to have his pistol confiscated? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that law, but if you didn't have a permit to carry your weapons, the weapons were confiscated and then legal proceedings were taken against that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I say that there were no criminal proceedings, just -- it was just considered a misdemeanor.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that I was a national deputy in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that I was the only deputy of the Serbian Radical Party in the National Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that you were the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, can you name someone else from the Serbian Radical Party then?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the Serbian Radical Party was established much later than all the other serious political parties in Serbia, only in February, at late as February 1991, in actual fact, with the unification of the Serbian Chetnik Movement and the popular Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that was the period when the party was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We didn't have an opportunity to go to the December elections in 1990; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It was only after subsequent elections that I won in Rakovica and became a deputy for my party; you don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj and Mr. Witness, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but again the interpreters are asking you to slow down because they have a hard time catching what you are saying when you overlap. So please respect a short pause between question and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As a deputy, I remember that it was only in the second half of 1992 that a law was passed about weapons and ammunition, which provided for criminal sanctions for illegal possession of weapons. Do you believe me when I say that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, the war circumstances and the arrival of a large number of refugees from the occupied Krajina territories brought in a large number of weapons into Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And people brandished weapons quite frequently in public places?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Before, we had settlings of account between criminals, usually brawls in cafes and drinking places. Suddenly we have conflicts between hundreds of people, and many people were killed with these strong musclemen, as they were called in the media, and groups like that of criminals and so on?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then there was increased use of weapons because people would just shoot up in the air, throw hand grenades in meadows during some celebrations or sometimes for no reason at all; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of examples like that, and they were shown on television, when birthdays were being celebrated, for example, that people who had weapons with them would use them to shoot, and people were injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember a fatal case when a stray bullet hit, I think, a young girl? I can't remember quite, but I think that was the case.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember something about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. So in that atmosphere, an atmosphere in which people brandished weapons very easily, without any reason, nobody took it up with anybody? Shooting all over the place, half an hour --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 30 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, when I'm driving, I don't need more than half an hour; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have such a good car, so I need more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I hope you'll be able to buy a better car and then you can drive faster. But don't drive too fast. Be careful about that. Anyway, under conditions like that, there was uncertainty among the population, regardless of nationality; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was one of the reasons, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: People felt far less safe than in the pre-war conditions, when there were rare cases of people being illegally in possession of weapons; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people felt far less safe because of the events that were happening in the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia, not because they were in possession of private sidearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mean the disintegration that was caused by the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A follow-up question, if I may. Through these questions, we understand that among those refugees, some had weapons, which didn't come out very clearly up until now. Now we know, we're sure about that. When these refugees came, after they were expelled from Croatia, I guess they were angry, because I guess they were not happy to have been expelled from their homes. You met these people, so what was your impression? Were they angry against Tudjman, who was forcing them to go, and/or were they angry against Slobodan Milosevic, who hadn't taken the necessary measures to protect them in Croatia so that they didn't have to leave? You were saying they had weapons. Of course, this state of mind could have led them to carry out certain types of activities. So who were they angry against? Were they angry against Tudjman, against Slobodan Milosevic, against the International Community which was not doing anything? Who were they angry against?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in my opinion by the talks I had with the refugees, they were angry with the Croatian government or, rather, Tudjman and Milosevic, or, rather, the Serb authorities who did not protect them sufficiently and for not having provided the circumstances for them to be able to stay in their households and their own thresholds. Now, as for the International Community, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Your answer is very clear. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that the Serb refugees were not satisfied with the conditions in which they were accommodated in Serbia and how the powers that be in Serbia took them in, received them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it your feeling that the authorities in Serbia didn't do everything they could to take into the refugees properly?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my feeling too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it your feeling that spontaneity was the main characteristic of the way in which the refugees were taken in? When I say "spontaneous," the local community did something, somebody did something over there, but there wasn't any systematic form of organisation to provide accommodation and welcome the refugees?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, what do you think, then?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there was spontaneous individual efforts, and in my -- the place I lived in, people took in refugees, but there were organised forms as well by the authorities to send refugees to certain areas where the inhabitants were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where do you get that information from?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's my conviction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you're speaking on the basis of your own conviction and not facts which could bear that out?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, facts -- well, if facts are not sent -- if refugees are not sent to areas in Serbia, but to Vojvodina, then this is a strong fact for me to base my opinion on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the refugees really did go all over Serbia and that there were reception centres in the south, in Vranje, Leskovac, Krusevac and so on?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, wouldn't it be normal for the refugees to try to find their own way, and the most logical solution, find a Croatian family with which to exchange their property? Would that be logical?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be normal and logical for the refugees to try and do something about their situation themselves, and there were many examples of that in Hrtkovci, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you agree that in Hrtkovci, a lot of property had already been exchanged in 1991, when the situation was calmer?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how many?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in comparison to the overall exchanges, perhaps 5 to 10 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Already in 1991, you say. All right, fine. Now, in 1992, you say that Ostoja Sibincic was a member of the Serbian Renewal Movement; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: To begin with, he was president of the local board?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But for a very short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you and Ostoja Sibincic were the main founders of the Serbian Renewal Movement in Hrtkovci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not right that we were the main founders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, not only you; there were others too? I've been asked to slow down again. We've been asked to slow down again. All right. Now, when the local board was formed, Ostoja Sibincic was elected president and you were elected secretary, so logically that would mean that the two of you were the main people in all that. There were other important people, but the two of you were the most important; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right, if you say so, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That means that you and Ostoja Sibincic were on very good terms. As far as I know, you were close friends at that time too.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you disbanded in 1992 the local board in Hrtkovci, you didn't inform the public about that at all, did you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not right. I did inform the public. I made a proclamation and sent out a letter to the Municipal Board in Ruma.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was that in the media at all?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, whether somebody published that in the media, I don't know, but I did put it up on the board as a proclamation and information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: My associates looked through all the daily papers from 1992, and they didn't find that piece of information, so the media ignored it, if you really did proclaim it yourself? Do you know that I made that proclamation, I provided that proclamation?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't found any information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, do you believe me when I say that I did that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me say that I do believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now, in 1992, the extraordinary elections were held, the federal, provincial, local and so on, in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That was in December?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In December, your party went to the elections, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you were a candidate for a municipal assemblyman on behalf of the SPO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If the local committee of the SPO is disbanded, how can you stand as a candidate and run in the election? I don't understand that. Well, it's not impossible, but could you explain how come that happened?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could have been a candidate in Ruma or anywhere else on behalf of my party. So according to our statute, it doesn't really matter whether there is a local committee, whether it had been disbanded or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please, let us be specific on this. The local elections were majority elections, meaning that the municipality of Ruma was divided into several election units. Hrtkovci was divided into two; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In one of these two units, you were the candidate of the SPO, the Serbian Renewal Movement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And your party was still strong enough for you to get into the second round; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The candidate running against you was a candidate of the Serbian Socialist Party, which was the ruling party at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he won over you only in the second round; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with a majority of only a few votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the candidate of the Serbian Radical Party won very few votes in the first round and did not get into the second round?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't get into the second round because refugees didn't have the right to vote. So it's only logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it's logical. You find it logical that that didn't happen, and that means also that the Serbian Radical Party wasn't all that popular in Hrtkovci yet; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the local population was concerned, it wasn't popular at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How did one acquire the right to vote in local elections? What was required? Just to reside there; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Nothing else is needed. You don't need any certificate of citizenship or anything of the kind?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the right to vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, there is a passive and an active right to vote; right? Passive is that someone can elect you, and active is that you can vote. For both active and passive voting rights, the same conditions were in force?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're not on the list of voters, you could not vote, and at that time the refugees came in and those who had exchanged houses didn't have the right to vote, and they were not registered in the voting lists. They could vote only in the next elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How come, as soon as they applied for residence in Ruma or, rather, in Hrtkovci, they have to be registered in the municipality and their right to vote, right, so somebody omitted to do that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps there were omissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: These omissions were, after all, of an individual nature, not en masse; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't know the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. But no certificate of citizenship was required at that time to participate in the elections, either to apply one's active or passive voting right; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first elections, I think that's the way it was. Already at the second elections, I had to have a certificate of citizenship.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That was later. I'm talking about 1992.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that later on many prominent opposition leaders first had to register in the book of citizens of Serbia and then only to exercise their voting rights? For example, Zoran Djindjic was born in Samac, Kostunica in Tuzla, Vuk Draskovic had his citizenship based in Gacko, where his father was born and where he grew up. They had to get citizenship of Serbia only at a subsequent date. Did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you know that Milan Panic did not have citizenship of Serbia, so it was only at a later stage that he had to register in the book of citizens?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So your party, at these elections in 1992, was still so strong in Hrtkovci that you got into the second round, and it was with great difficulty that the candidate of the Socialist Party won over you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My party did not have such large numbers, but it was big in --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Popularity?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You had a great deal of merit in the eyes of the voters; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, we were popular.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I know you were popular. That's what I'm talking about. All right. Ostoja Sibincic, when this local committee of the SPO was allegedly disbanded, up until 2000, did not join any other party; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was arrested twice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A follow-up question. I thought Mr. Seselj was going to ask it, but he didn't. This second round of election, there was only the Socialist Party and your party remaining. The candidate for the Serbian Radical Party didn't reach the second round. In your memory, the Serbian Radical Party got what kind of percentage of the votes during the election? Do you remember? If you know, of course. If not, then just let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't exactly, in percentage terms, but perhaps 50 or 60 votes. That's what the Serb Radical Party candidate won.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many votes did you win in the first round?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. Over a hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So more than twice as much as the candidate of the Radicals; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now you say that you do not remember. However, when you were making your statement to The Hague investigators in 2004 and 2006 -- twice; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In paragraph 10, you said, allegedly -- perhaps this is not correct, what they're stating there. I provide for that reservation, because I believe you more than I believe the investigators from The Hague. Do you believe me when I say that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It says here: "After the Hrtkovci SPO local board was dismantled, Ostoja Sibincic did not formally join any party until 1999-2000, when he became an SPS member in Ruma." They say that that's what you said. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you've refreshed my memory. I remember this one meeting of the SPS that I attended and where Sibincic's membership card was showed, because he joined in Ruma and according to the statute he was supposed to join the basic cell in his place of residence. They were opposed, so he was not accepted. That is the information that I received then, that he had joined the SPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was that in 1992 or 2000? So eight years after what had happened in Hrtkovci; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There are some speculations that after the SPS, he joined yet another party after 2000. Did you hear anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I know is that he is now in the Serb Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you said very nicely that it was only this year that he joined the Serb Radical Party or late in last year?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you were precise on that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In this seven-year intermezzo, was he a member anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear something, but I don't have any complete knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So what is it that you heard, because I heard that he made a new statement to my associates, but I haven't got it yet because they've imposed restrictions on me here.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. It doesn't really matter, then. Tell me, do you know how come Ostoja Sibincic became a member of the Serb Radical Party late last year?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, my investigators, Nemanja Sarovic and Elena Bozic-Talijan, have combed through Vojvodina, especially the municipality of Ruma, especially Hrtkovci, gathering information that is needed for my Defence, and the result of their work is this book of 1.200 densely-printed pages. That's the first time that they talked to Ostoja Sibincic, and that's when he made his first statement to them. A few days ago, he gave another statement to them, and it is after he talked to them that he decided to join the Serb Radical Party. Do you believe me when I say that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I heard in relation to Sibincic's membership was that he had blackmailed the municipal authorities to give them -- give him a job so that he'd make a statement pertaining to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How could he blackmail them when he worked for the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was an employee at the Revenues Department and then he was laid off as a redundant person, and later on he got a job as a clerk in the municipality, and it was the Serb Radical Party that was in power there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So then he blackmailed someone?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why would we allow anyone to blackmail us when people throughout Ruma and in Hrtkovci were actually rushing to my investigators and they could barely wait to talk to my investigators? Even you agreed to talk to Nemanja Sarovic, who did not know at all that you were an OTP witness; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, if it's not right. When you talked about these arrests of Ostoja Sibincic, you said at one moment when he got out of jail, he went on working at the Ruma municipality as if nothing had happened. You said something along those lines; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Could anyone actually dismiss him after the arrest and after the judgement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to go back to Sarovic. I'd like to refer you to line 4 of page 27. According to what Mr. Seselj says, his investigators did their work, and then Sarovic got in touch with you and at the time he didn't know you were an OTP witness. You're saying it's not true. This is on line 9, page 27 of the transcript. When Mr. Sarovic called you on the phone and when he met you, what did he tell you? Do you remember, specifically, what he said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my first contacts with Mr. Sarovic, he said to me that he wanted to talk to me in relation to my testimony against Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what he said, "I want to talk to you in relation to your testimony against Mr. Seselj"; is that what he told you, word for word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot remember exactly now because I do not remember, I mean, every little word exactly. Well, that's what he wanted to talk about, because he had had information that I was a Defence witness -- sorry, Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Since you've remembered all of this belatedly, tell me now, why did you state that Blagoje Dudic spoke at the rally of the Serb Radical Party in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not state that Blagoje Dudic spoke. As chairman, he's the one who announced who would be the speakers. He didn't speak, himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He didn't speak at all; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that he said anything, or if he did speak, I didn't really pay attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said here that he did speak, that he made a few introductory remarks. That's what you say in paragraph 41?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you stand by that or do you not remember? Perhaps you've forgotten. Things like that can be forgotten.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's been a long time, and as far as I can remember, that's the way it was, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. You spoke about this rally of citizens at the cultural centre in 1992, when the leadership of the local commune had been replaced or, rather, when they resigned and when a new leadership was elected, headed by Ostoja Sibincic; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said that Ostoja Sibincic was then illegally elected representative of the commune. Why?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I think that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, wait a minute. According to the laws in force then, were elections in local communes held at rallies of citizens?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the law then, it was by public vote, acclamation, or in writing at citizens' rallies. However, that was not a rally of the citizens of Hrtkovci only. It was a rally of citizens who came from elsewhere too. That is why I claim that it was illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who was it that established that there were citizens from elsewhere in attendance there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hall of the cultural centre takes a maximum of 250 people, and it was full of people standing in the aisles and in front and all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that your only argument when you say that there were quite a few citizens from elsewhere there as well?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time it wasn't customary for more than 50 or 60 per cent of the local population to respond to invitations to attend rallies and to have the local commune council elected in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When there is a rally, there's no need for a quorum; right? The number of citizens who show up actually make the decision; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Half an hour has to go by until there's a quorum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A quorum was not indispensable. One waits for half an hour from the scheduled time, and then work starts?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then work goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As if there were a quorum?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was the new leadership of the local commune elected unanimously?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know anyone who was there and who voted against the election of Ostoja Sibincic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to say something else in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You tell me what it is that I am asking you about. It's different when the Prosecutor is asking you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know, myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were you at that rally?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you vote against?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't vote in favour, so that means that I'm against.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That is not true. I am asking you whether you raised your hand to vote against him. You didn't; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no point in me raising my hand when the situation was as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When everybody was in favour of Ostoja Sibincic as president unanimously; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you speak at that rally of citizens?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke in front of the cultural centre at the rally of citizens that was held by the other inhabitants of Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who are these other inhabitants, other citizens?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time the citizens of Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Not with a single word did you oppose the election of Ostoja Sibincic as president of the local commune, although you were present at that rally of citizens, right, not a single word?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that kind of atmosphere was created of a verbal clash, with a possibility of it growing into a physical conflict, when I went out and when I asked the local inhabitants to walk out so that there wouldn't be a conflict, I think that that is a telling fact in its own right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No one remembers that you said a word, including asking anyone to leave. No one in Hrtkovci remembers that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if I understood well, this election had been rigged. Listening to you, it seems that there were people who were there, but they didn't have a right of vote. This is what you just told us; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness wasn't in a position to identify a single man who was not from Hrtkovci. His conclusion is on the basis of the large number, 200 and something-odd people who came to the meeting, that there must have been others on the side, because before 50 or 60 people would come to the rallies, citizens rallies. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Anyway, do you know about a single incident which happened in Hrtkovci between the refugees and the local population, any serious incident, where the police did not intervene when called? Can you tell me anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You can't remember because there were no such incidents. And do you know that in Ruma, the police of Serbia set up a separate headquarters, as it did in all other large places in Vojvodina, which was in charge of preventing incidents from breaking out in that generally heated atmosphere?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know, for example, that when the refugees entered houses that had been left void, empty houses, that the police always intervened whenever they were called and threw the refugees out of other people's houses?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that a certain Milivoj Vukelja, who tried to set up life in somebody else's house, was expelled to Republika Srpska; they went that far to expel him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Vukelja lived in that house for a few months, so it wasn't that he just tried to enter. He forcibly entered the house and lived there for a few months, and it was only after a court judgement that he was deported to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: With his family?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why was he deported to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I assume because it was considered that he wasn't from the areas from which the refugees had been expelled, but that he had come in from Bosnia and was therefore returned and deported back to Bosnia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you do know about the general situation; right. Now, why did you say that Slobodan Milosevic, with Tudjman, had reached an agreement on a population exchange? Where do you get that information from?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that that was my conviction, and I'm still convinced that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, if you're convinced of something, you must base that conviction on some facts. For example, I never saw anywhere in the press, or in the electronic media, or political rallies, that somebody accused Slobodan Milosevic of having agreed on a population exchange with Tudjman by way of expelling people.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my conclusion, and I base it on the events that took place and partially on information that was put out. You know that there was a secret meeting between Tudjman and Milosevic. You know that yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, we could have read a lot about that secret meeting in the media and some transcripts, too, but the media speculated that Tudjman and Milosevic had reached an agreement about carving up Bosnia. But nowhere did I read that they agreed about the exchange of the population between Croatia and Serbia. That was not in the media. So don't put this question on its head. If Tudjman -- if Tudjman and Milosevic discussed one question and reached an agreement about one question, you needn't draw the conclusion that they must have reached an agreement on a completely different issue because that's your opinion, that's your conviction.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that's my opinion, and I based it on the events that happened and the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Well, the Prosecution then has brought you in here to testify on the basis of your convictions. Well, that's possible, too. In The Hague Tribunal, things like that can happen too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you said this yesterday, sir, I was quite interested by this. Let's assume that what you said is right and that there is an agreement between Tudjman and Milosevic which will provide for the Serbs of Croatia to go to Serbia, and the other way around for the others. So the Croats who were in your own village, somebody has to tell them that they have to leave, in the framework of this agreement. So to your knowledge, the Croats who left, and I'm not talking about those who joined the Croatian National Guard but the others, were you convinced that some of those Croats left because someone had pushed them to leave, someone who was not a Serb, maybe he was a Croat, and who was exerting pressure in order to get them to leave so that the agreement would actually come to fruition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my assumption is based on the fact that there was information that I received from refugees who had exchanged their houses, and also on the basis of the events that took place in the place I lived in. And it is a fact that in Croatia, there was a civil war that happened, so there was an armed conflict at the very beginning between the authorities and the citizens. And in our state, that did not happen, and it is my opinion and my conviction that this is something that was coveted where we were, too. So the motive to send refugees to predominantly Croatian areas was that, too. On the basis of that, I base my opinions that there was an agreement to that effect, in actual fact, because in situations where there was force and violence, and when the population almost doubled, there was as many refugees as inhabitants in the area where I lived in, that interventions came too slow, and even where there was intervention, the perpetrator still stayed on in the town or village. So that led me to make that conclusion and form that opinion. Then and now, I understood the situation that these refugees were in. They were frustrated. Their properties had been destroyed. They'd been expelled. Family members had been killed. So I understand them, I understand their reactions. However, at the public rallies and when I spoke publicly, I always said that it wasn't the inhabitants of Hrtkovci who were to blame for what had happened "to you refugees, so don't blame them for your predicament."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I assume you know Croats who left, and maybe you talked to them because you had a good relationship with them as neighbours. I assume you did and you talked to them. So before they left, what did they tell you, if they told you anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, many people told me that when they had reported things to the police or went to the police or their friends' lawyers who had worked at the police force at one point or state institutions, that they were told that they couldn't protect them and that the best thing for them would be, for their own safety, to exchange their property. I also talked to many refugees, who told me why they were angry with me and those people that were protecting their neighbours. Well, the neighbours did not protect us there as you were neighbours protecting your neighbours here." That's what they said, so they expected me, as a member of the same ethnicity, should take them in, to forget my neighbours, the neighbours I lived next to and had lived for many years, just because the person was of Croatian or Hungarian ethnicity. They wanted me to go against my neighbours. So that's what I know about the situation, what they went through, how they came to leave and so on. What I want to say is this: I do have information that I received from the previous residents and inhabitants, that that was the case, that was how it was, and that the Serbs were not welcome there, returnees or any others, and they're not welcome to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Ejic, why, in your testimony, on many occasions do you mention the Hungarians? Have you ever heard of me or any other functionary of the Serbian Radical Party ever said an ugly word with respect to the Hungarians?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that's why I'm surprised that you're mentioning Hungarians at all in this context, in the context of you accusing me that I stoked the fire of the atmosphere to expel Croats. So there's no reason to mention Hungarians here, is there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the fact is it happened, so then there is grounds for mentioning Hungarians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, there were Hungarians in some places, too, but can that be linked to the policies waged by the Serbian Radical Party in any way?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were fewer exchanges with Hungarians in comparison to the Croatians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. I didn't understand that answer of yours, but never mind. You said that unconsciously I was a tool in the hands of Milosevic, which he used to promote his ends. Is that your conviction again or do you have facts to bear that out, to support that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my conviction on the basis of your behaviour and -- your behaviour in the press and in public. If you strive for the principle of reciprocity, then I cannot accept you as a humane person, because evil must not be met with evil.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So if I'm not a humane person, then according to you, I must be Milosevic's tool, because anybody who is inhumane is Milosevic's tool. Let aside the fact that you consider me to be inhumane, even if I were, if you consider me to be that, why would I have to be a tool in Milosevic's hands? Do you have any other reason for saying that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because you advocated the question of refugees most.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did do my best for refugees, and the Serbian Radical Party did strive for the principle of retorsion publicly, but we attacked Milosevic for not accepting that principle. Is that the truth of it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And we promised that when we came into power, we would apply that principle; is that true too?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And is everything we said in the pre-election campaign true, that we promised that when we came into power, we promised what we would do once we seized power; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was that too, there was that promise too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did you ever happen to hear me utter or anybody else utter from the Serbian Radical Party, high officials, that we advocated situations where incidents broke out, that the Croatian population should be abused and mistreated, that they should be beaten, that hand grenades should be thrown on their property and anything like that? Did you ever hear me utter things like that, or anybody from the party?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear of us giving out instructions of that kind clandestinely, secretly?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is just my assumption.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Your assumption; right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Seselj has put some questions to you on the retaliation principle, and I'm trying to shed some light on this. At the time, from what I understood out of what Mr. Seselj was saying, when he was talking about "retaliation or retorsion," what did that mean, as far as you were concerned? How far did it go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My understanding of the word is that it is a response to the conduct and behaviour of a state, the authorities, towards a section of the population, and that the same conduct should be applied in the other state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does this mean that this led to the following situation, and I'll illustrate this with an example: A Serb is expelled by a Croat. Does this automatically lead to the fact that a Croat will be expelled by a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is how you understand it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, since you understood it that way on the basis of the leading question put to you by the Presiding Judge, were you conscious at the relevant time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you're not allowed to say this, it's a leading question. I put a question to the witness, and I'm entitled to ask any question I wish. Secondly, I wanted to know from the witness what he met by retribution, the principle of retribution. I shall give an example, practical case, and he gave us an answer. So let's not make anything out of this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: At the relevant time, did I speak about the state policy and not what one individual did was something that another individual did? I was talking about state policy, "When we come into power, we will provide you with the addresses, and then you will exchange your property with them." Did I say that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did say that, but the inhabitants didn't understand that that was something that would be applied before you came into power.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But that was the policy of the Serbian Renewal Movement, led by you and Ostoja Sibincic, and not the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know of a single case whereby the members of the Serbian Radical Party from Hrtkovci exerted pressure on the local Croats to move out, a single case? Give me the name and surname of somebody who was a member of the Serbian Radical Party who did things like that.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was an official member at the time, but, for example, what happened to my cousin -- to my brother-in-law by Cakmak and his son and somebody else tells me that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But Rade Cakmak was never a member of the Serbian Radical Party. Ostoja Sibincic became a member at the end of last year, but Rade Cakmak never was.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the prevailing opinion, that they were members of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see. So whenever a Serb does something bad, you are convinced straight away that that person must be a member of the Serbian Radical Party; is that the logic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the logic, but if the Serbian Radical Party did nothing in the local area and let incidents like that go by, then that's the opinion I draw.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Hague Tribunal has several speeches of mine in which I speak out against incidents like that, and they must have put out a proclamation on -- up on the board; right? So what newspaper would be interested about what a local board does in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public board for announcements in Hrtkovci is not a yard fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. You said that Ostoja Sibincic, in 1992, was arrested pursuant to instructions from the federal Prime Minister Milan Panic; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard. That's what the press wrote about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On what grounds? On what grounds was the prime minister able to give instructions for anybody's arrest? Where is that to be found in the law?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't understand the law, but you say he issued instructions to that effect?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I know that there was a lot of problems in Serbia with the functioning of the legal system, but that a prime minister can order somebody's arrest in Serbia, that was absolutely impossible, right, especially as that federal prime minister was in a conflict with the president of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The arrest did happen now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, yesterday when you said this, I was quite surprised. I wondered how a federal prime minister could take care of what was happening to John Doe at some kind of village. I was quite surprised. And you say, "I heard," but through hearsay or what, because you had no specific elements that could lead you to think that Milan Panic had arrested Ostoja Sibincic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Your Honour, that this is what was written in some newspapers, and Mr. Panic himself spoke on television to the effect -- well, I can't remember his exact words. Now, did he suggest or order the arrest?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But if Panic talked about it over the television, why was Sibincic arrested? What was the motivation behind arresting this person? He was against law and order, he was an agitator; why did he want him arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, because Mr. Panic himself had received information and complaints from the citizens of Hrtkovci that Ostoja Sibincic, together with a group of refugees, was the organiser and protagonist of all of these things that were happening in Hrtkovci; violence, threats, evictions of people from houses, forcible moving in and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I understand better now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When talking to The Hague investigators, you stated that at one moment a group of people from elsewhere showed up, who exerted pressure, and you said that they were either Arkan's men or White Eagles. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When was this? Just the year, just the year. The date doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that year, 1992. I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And on the basis of what did you conclude that they were Arkan's men or White Eagles? Did they have some insignia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't even see them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Somebody told you that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who it was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Do we have enough time until the break? I want to put one more question. I hope there's enough time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can extend the time for four or five minutes, if so required by this question, perhaps. Do you allow me to do that? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, towards the end of your statement to The Hague investigators, you said or you mentioned that I also had a gathering within the local elections campaign in Ruma and in Indija, that I criticised Slobodan Milosevic and the Socialist Party there, as well as Vuk Draskovic and the Serbian Renewal Movement, and that at these two gatherings I said that all of those who were not local Serbs should leave, and you ascribed other things to me as well. Do you remember having said that to The Hague investigators?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, correction in relation to that. I do remember, but I attended two gatherings, one in Ruma and another one in Indija. I don't remember what the date was. I know that the one in Indija was held on a Sunday, because I played chess at the club there. I stand corrected in relation to whether you took part in these two gatherings or was it only your party and its representatives. Perhaps I confused this with your speeches on television, so then I linked it up to these two cases when I was actually present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A few days ago, on the 5th of October, you talked again to the Prosecutor, to the investigators from The Hague, and as far as they've informed me, you stated that you were not sure whether Seselj took part at the gatherings in Ruma and Indija or whether it was on television that he had seen Seselj: "He had seen a large number of meetings on television, so perhaps he was confused. Nikolic, the former deputy, spoke. He remembers that that person spoke in Ruma and Indija. The witness attended these two meetings. The meeting in Indija was on a Sunday at 1.00 or 2.00 in the afternoon. The one at Ruma was held later at 6.00. He wasn't sure whether Seselj was present or not. The meeting was organised by the SRS, but he's not sure whether Seselj was present." What was it that happened on the 5th of October that you mentioned that Tomislav Nikolic spoke at these two gatherings?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are a lot of things that I saw on TV, so I confuse things in terms of my memory.
