Since I do not remember faces and people that much, I remember the essence of what happened and what was spoken in general terms, so that's why I said that, that I'm not sure whether you were there or not, whether I confused you with being there or being on television, and then I linked those two up or, rather, these two gatherings that I personally attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you do not know that at that time, Tomislav Nikolic lived in Kragujevac, and that he only attended big rallies of the Serb Radical Party in Sumadija, Pomoravlje, and he attended smaller ones, that was his area and and elsewhere in Serbia, he attended only big rallies? What I'm saying to you is it is impossible that Tomislav Nikolic spoke in Ruma and Indija, because these are, after all, small towns and he wouldn't come all the way from Kraljevac to be there. Do you believe me when Ii say that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can believe you, and it's possible that I got mixed up in terms of faces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The fact that Tomislav Nikolic was thrown out of the Serb Radical Party, is that what perhaps made you say to The Hague investigators, "Ah, he spoke at these rallies"?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was the association maybe that now Tomislav Nikolic is moving in the steps of Vuk Draskovic, your former president, and that you inferred it on the basis of that? I'm really surprised why you mentioned his name here.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned his name as a prominent official of --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that's a bit irresponsible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Trial Chamber has asked you not to address Mr. Nikolic's situation in relation to your own party. Everyone is well aware of this. We don't need to rehash the subject over and over again. The only important question was to find out whether Mr. Nikolic had actually made this speech. It seems that the witness is no longer sure about this, so please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on the 5th of October, the witness was sure, when he spoke to the investigators from The Hague, or the Prosecutor, or whoever it was that talked to him. He is sure here Nikolic, the former deputy, spoke. That is what is written here on page 3 of this document that I received from the OTP: "Present were the following persons:"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But what is important is what the witness is saying today in this courtroom before the Bench.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Ms. Lattanzi, it is important when I see that there is a collision between his two statements, what he says today and what he says four days ago. What's the day today, the 9th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but he admitted, he said that he might have been confused. He gave us an explanation, and that is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, on the basis of similar confused witnesses yesterday, Milan Martic, the president of the Republic of the Serb Krajina had his sentence of 35 years confirmed. A witness gets confused, and terrible things happen. I have the right to defend myself in this way, and it only suits me when witnesses get confused, so I try to use it to a maximum. As far as I'm concerned, you can take the break now, if that's what you wanted. Just tell me how much more time I have left. I have two or three questions left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You must have -- well, we'll take a break, of course, but you will have one hour left after the break, one hour. We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're back in session. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor. I told you you had one hour left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I'll finish even a bit earlier. Some important questions will remain unanswered, because I have to remind you yet again that I have not been allowed contact with my associates. So as for cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I think we have been through this before, and you are incorrect in saying that you have been denied access. The only thing is that you have still the possibility of contacting your Defence associates in Belgrade, but not under the privileged terms, because the issue of a possible violation is still pending.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I don't have a privileged relationship, then it's as if I had no relationship whatsoever, and indeed I do not have any relationship. So I have to remind you, each and every time I cross-examine, that that is the case. Well, you can forbid that as well, because that is a problem for me for as long as witnesses are here, and I do have the right to complain for being denied the possibility of putting more important questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ejic, sometime in mid-1992, you got in touch with Nenad Canak, president of the Legal of Social Democrats in Vojvodina; right? When did that take place?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please ask you not to speak so loud, because I really cannot handle it even through headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, move them away. What can I do about it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. It is correct that I had contacts with Nenad Canak. This was after the killing of Mijat Stefanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mijat Stefanac was killed during the night between the 28th and 29th of June, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly what the date was. Approximately that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the murderers were killed immediately on that day, that they were taken to court and convicted?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What was the reason for you to go to see Nenad Canak; the fact that Stefanac was killed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So what did you say to Canak then?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited him at his apartment. I informed him about the situation in Hrtkovci, and I mentioned that I was very frightened that the first murder had happened. The motive was not known, but the fact remains that this did happen, and that I was afraid that similar situations could spread.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who got you in touch with Nenad Canak?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but somehow I managed to get his telephone number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you call him up then and say, "This is who I am, my name is" so-and-so, "I wish to talk to you"? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I that think we've known each other from earlier on, from the public domain. He knew my name and I knew his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How is it you met?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that is a very prominent figure in Serbian political life. I, for instance, remember when I first met him, although as a politician he's not all that important, but then I remember and you don't remember. I find that a bit strange. Right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't find it strange. Sometimes I forget my very own neighbour's real name and then I remember it afterwards, and especially now, after all this time, I cannot remember all these details that are not really important in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, wasn't it more natural for you to call the president of your own party at the time, Vuk Draskovic, and to discuss what had happened with him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would have been more natural. However, when I disbanded the local board, I, in fact, ceased being a member and I was no longer active in the SPO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But this is the month of June. In June, you hadn't disbanded the board yet. It was in the second half of the year that you did that; right? That's what you said. You went to see Nenad Canak at the time when you were still president of the local board of the Serb Renewal Movement; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that that's exactly the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When did you disband the local board of the SPO?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I don't even remember that date. If you remind me with a document, then I can confirm, yes, that's when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said the end of 1992. I would like to remind you of what you, yourself, said. What do I need documents for? What you pasted on that bulletin board of yours there is something that I've never seen, and no one remembers that. You said yourself that at the end of 1992, you disbanded the local board of the SPO and that you had the consent of the Municipal Board to do that, and that is something that remains carved in one's memory forever. That party of yours disappeared in Hrtkovci then and it was never renewed, although as a candidate of that party in December 1992, you ran in the election, and after that you were even a candidate in the provincial elections; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remembered that what remains carved in my memory are events and facts, not dates and names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. What was it that Nenad Canak said to you then, when you explained the situation in Hrtkovci to him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he said that he could not help me very much because pressure is being brought to bear against him, too, by the authorities. He just made it possible for me to have contacts with the press. I think it was Mazar Sol [phoen] and some other media. I can't remember exactly now. I went there and I made a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Ejic, Nenad Canak at the time was the president of a marginal political party which was not represented at all either in the Federal Parliament or the Republican Parliament, and at no local level of government either; right? They had no municipal assemblymen, no MPs, no one. You went to see this very marginal politician to seek his intervention and assistance, and the president of your party, in Belgrade -- Belgrade is closer to you than Novi Sad. The president of your party is there, and your party at that time was a major opposition party; right? In the Parliament of Serbia, your party had the largest number of MPs, compared to other opposition parties; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Isn't that a bit strange?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps to you, but not to me, because I went to see a man who's from Vojvodina and who was opposed to what was happening in Vojvodina, so I don't find that strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Ejic, you were afraid of the policy you had been pursuing until then because a man had lost his life. You were not aware of the circumstances of his death, and you were seeking ways and means to get yourself out of that situation, and that is why you did not turn to the organs of your party that stood behind what had happened in Hrtkovci. Rather, you sought Nenad Canak, knowing, although his party was way too small, that he had lots of contacts with the media, especially foreign journalists, that he also had diplomatic contacts and so on and so forth, not to go into any depth; right? You wanted in a way to switch sides on time?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't see any question in this long speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, this is the first objection raised today, and I hope it will be the last. Please try to turn what you've just said into a question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think the question was a very clear one and a precise one, and I'm not going to repeat it. I'm going to move on to my other question, and it is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, don't feel offended. You have the screen in front of you. Look at line 1, page 52. You can see that it's more a statement than a question. If you don't want to ask that question, fine, but this is the reason why Mr. Ferrara raised his objection, and I think he was right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, if he was right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Ejic, what else did Nenad Canak do with respect to your arrival?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to enabling me to have access to the media and make a statement, he did his best to inform the public and the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then you made an agreement with Nenad Canak that all the blame should be placed on the Serbian Radical Party, shifted to them, because the killing of Mijat Stefanac you were sure would have serious consequences; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't reach any agreement with anybody linked to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Not me, personally, but the Serbian Radical Party. Anyway, Nenad Canak, did he send out a large number of journalists, both foreign and domestic, to Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is that after that event, a large number of domestic and foreign journalists did appear in our town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And a campaign against the Serbian Radical Party was unleashed; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand it that way, as a campaign against your party at the time, but as informing the broader public about what was happening in Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And it was orchestrated, synchronised, all the problems in Hrtkovci were made to appear as being the consequence of my 6th of May speech at a Serbian Radical Party meeting; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did any other famous people come to Hrtkovci during that time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you refresh my memory and give me a name, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Did Natasa Kandic, for instance, come to Hrtkovci immediately after that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know she was there, but I don't know whether she came immediately afterwards, and I fairly frequently had contacts with her, too, with respect to the situation in Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many times did you have -- were you in contact with her?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite a number of times. I can't remember how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When was the last time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a few years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you talk to Natasa Kandic about your testimony in the trial against me?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't; right. Now, what about Vesna Pesic, the president of the Citizens Alliance or the Reformist Party; did she come to Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a citizens' rally, there were a number of representatives, I remember on one occasion, and I remember the Seselj Democratic League, the party of Vojvodina Croats, and Hungarians, the Citizens Alliance and so on. Now, whether Vesna Pesic was there, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, do you know that Vesna Pesic convinced Dr. Branimir Vuksanovic that his name should be found on a secret list for persecution and that he should leave Hrtkovci as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you claimed here that Mr. Zilic, among other things, at a rally mentioned the name of Branimir Vuksanic; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And nobody heard that except for you, nobody remembers that, no the policemen who were present, and yesterday I quoted a passage of the Security Service detail that was there. Nobody mentions that the name of Branimir Vuksanic was mentioned at all. What do you say to that? Branimir Vuksanic is one of the most prominent and respected citizens of Hrtkovci; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a doctor, yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was a very well-loved doctor. He was recognised as a good diagnostician, his wife was a Serb, and he was on good terms with everyone. He was never involved in any incidents.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think his wife is still a Serb and what you say is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And this group chose him to provide him with false information and to encourage him to leave Hrtkovci and to exchange his property for a suburb of Zagreb or somewhere around Zagreb, and to influence other Croats to do the same through his example, to exchange their own properties?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know of a single incident linked to the name of Branimir Vuksanic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I heard from him personally was that at his workplace, he had an unpleasant time when he heard comments made by others to the effect, "I don't want to be treated by an Ustasha doctor," and things like that, and that he was threatened through the mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how come he doesn't remember that, that people said they didn't want to be treated by an Ustasha doctor? Nobody ever referred to him as a Ustasha in Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember [as interpreted] how he doesn't remember, because that's how the story went, how I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. You looked through this list provided to you by the OTP, isn't that right, and on the list we have 728 names of Croats from Hrtkovci; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, and the names I added.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: 722, and you added 6 names to the list; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You established, first of all, that all the people on the list had not actually moved out of Hrtkovci and that some live there today still?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then you marked a total of eight people who you thought had left under pressure; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I, yes, made a note of eight, singled out eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The first name is Branko, Branimir Vuksanic, I don't know what his real name was, and Nikola Vuksanic; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And as to pressure exerted against them, you give the example of the fact that somebody had said to him at work that he didn't want to be treated by an Ustasha doctor; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the threat, the pamphlet put through his letter box?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, pamphlet through the letter box.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Pakic, Rozalija and Vlado, what about them? That was a married couple from Skolska [phoen] Street who were forcibly evicted by the refugees, but were returned to their homes with the help of the police; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are they still living in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they're still living in Hrtkovci today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So they had a problem. The police resolved that problem, and they've stayed on living there. Were all the rest able to stay on? If they had some unpleasantness, they got through it; they would contact the authorities and be given protection. Was that the normal way of doing things, going about things?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it should have been, but it wasn't like that in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then we have the couple Jelica and Franjo Tkalac; right? You said that a hand grenade was thrown next to their house?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say that now, too, and that's what I wrote on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. It probably was a hand grenade. I heard that there were three or four hand grenades or, rather, explosions in Hrtkovci. To my knowledge, four, in fact, and you mentioned three explosions. That's no secret. Now, tell me what happened to that couple?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They live in Croatia today and exchanged their property.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who did they exchange their house with?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With refugees from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did they receive property which was worth more or less, in relation to the value of the property they owned?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they didn't complain to me that they had been short-changed at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: According to my information, they received property of far greater value than their original property in Hrtkovci. Right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some cases, what you say was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The seventh example of pressure that you mention is Josip Bagi?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Josip Bagi. He is my brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you spoke of the incident that took place?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Anyway, did Josip Bagi continue to live in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he still lives in Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the eighth name that pressure was exerted upon was you, Aleksa Ejic; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So to the best of your knowledge, those were all the people from Hrtkovci upon whom pressure was brought to bear; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not quite right. They were people that I know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, that you know about. Well, had you known of other cases, I'm sure you would have marked their names on this list. You wouldn't have kept quiet about them.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what you hear from others, you can't actually claim to be 100 per cent true, so that is why I didn't pinpoint any other names, except for the fact that I added that the other names, the names of other people, due to psychological pressure, entered the exchange process.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But this psychological pressure was created by the general mood in the society?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There weren't specific instances of pressure or coercion, people saying, "You have to leave and move out or we'll kill you;" do you agree with what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, partially.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can we then say that the Croatian population in Hrtkovci, some organised force launched an attack, and that it was as a result of an attack that they left their houses and flats and fled?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if by "organised force" you consider a group of five or six citizens, then that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you consider that in Hrtkovci, a crime against humanity was committed against the Croats of Hrtkovci? Do you know what a crime against humanity means, that term, do you know what it means?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand it, "crime against humanity" means inhumane treatment, violence, physical and psychological pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the consequences must be terrible for it to be a crime against humanity; right? Anyway, that's an expert question. Let's leave that for the moment. Do you consider that in any one case, that members of the Croatian National Minority [as interpreted] in Hrtkovci or any other place in Vojvodina, that deportation was carried out? Do you know what "deportation" means, when you capture somebody, take them into custody, and then deport that person somewhere, just like when they arrest the Romany ethnicity in Germany and deport them to Serbia? That's an example of deportation. Were there any instances of a single Croat being deported from Serbia to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And can you mention a single case of forcible eviction -- or let me explain the difference between deportation and forcible expulsion. Deportation is between states, and forcible expulsion or eviction is within one state. Have you got any examples of somebody coming and telling someone, "You now have to move to some other place in Belgrade," Novi Sad or wherever, and forcibly force that person to pick up all his chattels and move out; any examples?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The example of Milivoj Vukelja is a case in point, and when there was a Serb decision to move him out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But they were Serb refugees. Just a moment, I'm talking about Croats now. Do you have a single case of a Croat that was forcibly expelled and forced to move and settle somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not for deportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you've understood the difference between deportation and forcible expulsion. It's only of a formal nature?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, many Croats were motivated -- now, I'm going to put this to you, and then you can say whether you agree with me or not. Many Croats were motivated to exchange their properties. One of the reasons were that they would be exchanging their own property for property of greater value. The second reason was that they considered that their life would be better in Croatia than it would be in Serbia. The third reason was that they were afraid of social disruptions in Serbia because a vast -- a large wave of refugees had already arrived in Serbia, so their future was not certain. The fourth reason was that perhaps they had experienced some incident -- an incident, whether serious or less serious. The police intervened in all these incidents, but people perhaps thought it would be better to exchange their properties than run any risks. So now have I quoted the four main reasons for people engaging in an exchange of property?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have, you have set out the main reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, fine. Then that concludes the cross-examination, and, Mr. Ejic, I have no reason to be dissatisfied with your testimony at all, and I wish to state that publicly, and any negative reaction in your environment towards you would be ill-intentioned, and if it were to occur, I would condemn it. So there's no reason for that at all, sir, and I don't think you have any reason to fear anything. That is my personal view.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for being -- if you're frank and sincere.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you doubted my frankness and sincerity, I doubted yours. But we're on opposite sides, you're a Prosecution witness, I'm the accused, so that's something that's quite normal. But I really think that there's no reason for you to fear because you've helped me a great deal in presenting some of the information and details you've gave here, especially with helping me to identify the people for whom you establish that pressure was exerted upon them, including the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I came here to tell the truth and the whole truth of what happened, and that is my motive for coming here; nothing else. And of course we differ politically, we have different opinions and views as to how the situation should have been dealt with and how the situation should be dealt with today, indeed, and that's the basic difference between you and me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a few follow-up questions. I take the opportunity of you being here to try and better understand a few aspects of the indictment and the pre-trial brief. The Prosecutor and Mr. Seselj brought out this speech made on the 6th of May, 1992, by Mr. Seselj, but I'm looking at the indictment and the pre-trial brief, and I notice that we needed to go back even further in time. According to what the Prosecutor claims, and of course the Prosecutor's claims will be put under scrutiny when the Judges deliberate, but what the Prosecutor says is that during the fall of 1991, before May 1992, in other words, another speech was delivered by Mr. Seselj in Subotica, in Vojvodina. Had you heard about that speech? Did you hear that it had been delivered?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately I cannot recall anything in relation to that speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is the starting point for the Prosecutor. This is in paragraph 126 of the Prosecutor's brief. You don't have it, but trust me, I'm quoting from that document. With the influx of Serb refugees, there was also a campaign of intimidation of non-Serbs in several municipalities of Vojvodina, and in particular in your own area. Now, as far as you know, did other people, maybe other members of your own party, tell you that this was the same situation everywhere, that there were several campaigns of intimidation, or didn't you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I didn't know anything about it. I knew that there were stories of that nature and that there was that kind of campaign going on too, but I don't have any personal knowledge. It wasn't that I was present or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You'd heard several things, but you didn't have personal knowledge. Fine. Still, according to the Prosecutor, members of the Serbian Radical Party from the municipality of Sid, the stronghold of the party, according to you, were all the members of the party concentrated in Sid, at least most of them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that we in Sid also had a strong organisation, and once I even attended a meeting there, which is to say that the SPO had quite a presence in Sid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] SPO was very present in Sid. Now, to your knowledge, did Mr. Seselj's supporters or those who were in his movement, were they also -- was there a strong presence of these people in Sid.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't know. Because paragraph 126 of the Prosecution's brief, the Prosecutor says that members of the Serbian Radical Party of Sid used to roam around in cities and villages, it does seem that there are a lot of people who are roaming around in cities and the villages to harass the Croats. So if this is true, if what is alleged here is true, you know, we will be asking all these questions to other witnesses, not just you, but we have a person here in the courtroom who has good information on this, so let's take advantage of this. So could you tell us whether at the time you knew that there were these harassment and intimidation campaigns going on in cities and villages in the area?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I heard that something like that had been written in the press; namely, that certain groups were doing things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the press. Very well, in the press, only in the press. How far is Sid from Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 40 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 40 kilometres. Very well. There was mention of the Hungarians who lived in your village. How far is the Hungarian border from Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Novi Sad is 60 kilometres away, and then Subotica, say, about 100 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Croats who'd left for Croatia and who came back later on, because we know that when things cooled down, some Croats came back, and you actually told us that some Croats had come about, now, did you discuss with those who returned, did you discuss these events with them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question. You mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me be very specific. There were Croats who used to live in your village, and in 1992 they left that town to go to Croatia, maybe Zagreb or elsewhere. They went to Croatia. So either that was in the framework of a voluntary flat exchange or because of exchanges that had been initiated by someone. So all these people left for Croatia, and then a few years later, when things cooled down, these people came back, and I thought, if I'm not mistaken, that you did say that some came back. Now, did you discuss it with those who actually came back?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilic, Justina, is a person who is deceased. She left. She carried out an exchange of her house. She left with her husband, and her daughter stayed on in Platicevo, and then she returned and lived with her daughter. I know of that case. What I mentioned was that some people had left and then returned. I meant they went somewhere abroad, sought shelter somewhere, and then returned afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm interested in is those Croats who went to Croatia, not those who went abroad. Those who went to Croatia and came back, were there any of them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the question, and I mentioned this one case that I'm aware of of this elderly person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you discuss with this elderly lady, did you discuss the events with her.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometimes we did talk, and she expressed her dissatisfaction and her regret over the fact that she had left in the first place and carried out the exchange. Specifically, she had carried out an exchange for a home at a smaller place. I think it's Kula. In relation to Hrtkovci, it's not as nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This exchange of houses, which we've already discussed with other witnesses, it's not extremely clear in my mind, and maybe also in the mind of my fellow Judges. So you exchange houses. Does this mean that you exchange them over a period of time or that you actually own the house? Because if you become owner of the house, there needs to be some kind of deed. So how did it happen? I mean, you were a local official. You were well informed on many things, and you proved this amply to us. So when there is a house exchange, what happens regarding the deeds?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, exchange procedures evolved as follows: Refugees, well, many of them used the telephone to agree on exchanges. However, there were examples of the residents of Hrtkovci going out there to check things out and carry out exchanges only then. There were many agreements of that kind. They would make an agreement over the telephone, they would take each other's word, and that's what they'd do. And then this would be made official at the court in the municipality of Ruma, this official document on the exchange of the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you go to the municipality or to court. I believe I've heard that. And that's when the official document on the exchange of the house is actually drafted; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I assume that the Croats going to Zagreb also need to draft an official deed in order to exchange the vacant Serb house, so are there two official deeds that are done simultaneously or is there only one deed.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, I think that this was not possible for many people because of the war operations in Croatia, to do that. It was only done through -- in Serbia, but then perhaps the document would be dealt with through a lawyer in Croatia as well, and it would be verified in that way. I know many people did not go there because of their personal safety concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In passing again, a very interesting detail. You said that people were calling on the phone. So they call on the phone, they make an agreement over the phone, and sometimes they even go on site to check the house. Very well. Let's imagine that we have Mr. X living in Zagreb. He's a Serb, and he will call Mr. Y, who is a Croat living in Hrtkovci. And over the phone, they say, "Can we exchange houses?" So everything happens over the phone, if I understood you well.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know the case of Milan Fumic, that he spoke on the telephone with the current owner, Zunic, who was staying with some relatives or friends of his in Vojvodina at the time. I heard that from Zunic as well, that it was over the telephone that they carried out the exchange or, rather, agreed on it. Milan Fumic went to the actual spot, saw the property involved, and then he returned and wrote up a deed in Ruma.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And when those who arrived found out that they had a nice house earlier and that they were stuck now with a smaller house that was not so nice, what happened ?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many people didn't have a choice. Then they accepted what was offered to them at that point in time, although they were not satisfied with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What of today?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were cases the other way around, too, from the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had a question for you, but I saw Mr. Seselj raising his hand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm trying to contribute to this very good examination of yours. I think it would be a good thing to see exactly who the people who did not have a choice were. Was it the Croats from Serbia who were exchanging property with the expelled Serbs, or the Serbs who were expelled from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You did say that earlier. It didn't escape me. It looked like at first some did this on a voluntary basis, very freely, but then some really didn't have much of a choice. So the Serbs who lived in Croatia -- you know, our problem is that in the evidence that we were provided with, we don't really know what the situation in Croatia was. We have a few elements in this respect, but not much. We don't really know what happened over there. So the Serbs in Croatia who would -- so this Mr. X in Croatia, who is calling Mr. Y in Hrtkovci, Mr. X is a Serb living in Croatia and he's calling, does he calling because he's forced by the Croats to do this? This is important.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, precisely on account of that, that he was forced to do something like that, and that was the situation of the locals of Hrtkovci. When they were carrying out an exchange, it wasn't that they were forced to do that by the person with whom they were carrying out the exchange, but they had clashed with somebody else. There were examples on both sides. There were more examples from the Croat side --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the rest of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me return to your assumption, the fact that there would have been an agreement between Tudjman and Milosevic, because that might explain some things if it's true. So far, we have no elements, but just like Diogenes, I'm trying to -- with my lantern, I'm trying to find explanations. So those Serbs are calling over the phone. I would like to know whether they called the Croats in Hrtkovci first or whether it was the other way around, whether it's the Croats in Hrtkovci that called the Serbs. Who called first, according to you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, the first exchanges took place, well, not when the refugees arrived en masse, but when the refugees arrived from the areas where there were no war operations in Croatia, that is to say, when they arrived from Zagreb and the other towns. I think that I have mentioned two examples already of the Jogar family with Ulemek and the Udenko [phoen] family with Sulan. They were among the first to carry out this exchange, so it was the other way around. In Croatia, they had been contacted by some persons or they received threats to the effect that they should carry out an exchange with such-and-such a person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was before the tension. It was peaceful, and that's when there was these early exchanges?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It first started from the Croatian side. Serbs were seeking to carry out exchanges with Croats in Hrtkovci and in other places, that is to say, once they had already arrived. It's not that they had contacted the Croats in Hrtkovci from Croatia, and it's not that exchange offers were made then. They were already in Serbia, in different places, Hrtkovci included. Your Honour, one more thing in relation to this thesis. One of the arguments in relation to this plan would be the following: At a meeting, at a conference, a press conference, when the Minister of Human Rights, Ms. Margit Savovic was there, I wanted to attend. However, the organiser, President Sibincic at the time, demanded that I leave. He was probably afraid that I would tell the truth as to what was going on in Hrtkovci. So, in fact, as Minister of Human Rights, she was supposed to meet with the persons who were imperiled, not by those who were imperilling them. At the exit, she asked me, "Mr. Ejic, what is it you have against the refugees?" I gave her a brief answer, "Madam, I have nothing against refugees, nor did I ever have anything against them. I am only opposed to what they are doing, that is to say, instigating violence, carrying out violence, threats, things like that." That's the only thing I said. I did not get an answer to this comment of mine. I expected her to contact me after the meeting or, rather, to -- that she would ask to talk to us who had made statements to the press. That never happened. That supports my thesis that there had been an agreement with the authorities to act that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. The situation today in your village, is everyone good friends with Mr. Sibincic, are things -- is the relationship correct? Now that things have cooled down, is everybody, you know, friendly or is there still some problems that haven't been solved, like people who left and exchanges that haven't finished? What is your assessment of the situation as it is now in your village?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation in the village now can be termed as normal. Time has passed, and many people who were frustrated at the time and who did not think kindly of the Croats and the Hungarians have changed their minds in the meantime. Now they are friends with many of them. I'm also on good terms with the majority, as opposed to some people, individuals, who were extremists. That can be found at any time, but they are exceptions to the rule. I even won over their confidence, so for a while I was even president of the Council of the Local Commune for over four years, so that was one and a half terms of office. I did many things during that period of time. I made it possible to build a refugee settlement, too. The current situation can be described as normal, in the briefest possible terms. You mentioned Ostoja Sibincic. I am sorry that he's very ill. Now he is being avoided by refugees and locals because of the activities that he had engaged in. Generally speaking, the situation is normal. Right now, there are local elections for the municipality, and previously there had been elections for the local commune. It is a fact that there is just one representative of the Radical Party in local government. All the rest belong to local parties. That shows that the situation is normal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One final question. It's a bit sensitive, but I need to ask it, because you are an official, you were elected. You know what happened. According to you, what does a resident of your village feel, as far as this Tribunal is concerned? Are they defiant, do they trust the Tribunal? What is the feeling of the residents of your town regarding this institution?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, my knowledge and my opinion is that opinions are divided on the basis of the fact that some of the accused have been acquitted, although they committed crimes against the Serb population. So that's why opinions are divided. However, I personally trust this Tribunal. That is why I came to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for your answer. I believe my fellow Judges also have questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ejic, the only question I had for you is if you know whether the exchange of property between refugees from Croatia and refugees from Hrtkovci, whether these exchanges were organised by any institution, or did they occur spontaneously by rumour or by information that was just spread around among the people that, you know, they could just try and call some contacts in the other end of their journey and see if they could get into contact with somebody who was leaving there? That would be one way. The other way would be if there was an organisation somehow that was in charge of the process of putting people together for them to arrange for an exchange of property. Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question, Your Honour. My view of that matter is that most of these cases were spontaneous. There is quite a bit of knowledge on both sides, to the effect that certain groups that were self-organised gathered information about addresses and forwarded that to refugees. So in this way, they led them to the possibility of exchanges. I mentioned who was doing that in our village. I don't know about Croatia, but I did know that that kind of thing did exist; namely, that they provided addresses there of the Serbs with whom exchanges could be carried out. They gave them to Croats in Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And these self-organised groups, were they affiliated to any organisation or movements?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, two days ago you -- when we were talking about these exchanges, you mentioned fake contracts that had been drafted. Could you give us some details on this, be more specific on this? I did not really understand what you meant at the time with these fake contracts, and I would like to know where the pressure to draft these fake contracts actually came from.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, I think that it is Rade Cakmak. Now, who gave him this idea, to the best of my knowledge, it was Ostoja Sibincic, who prompted others to act in the same way as well. It was only when the real owner appeared and started proceedings before a court of law people found out that they had shown to the police this kind of fake contracts, because the police would not intervene until the real owner complained to a court of law. That is what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't really understood yet. There were contracts which mentioned owners who were not the real owners who actually took over the house; is that it? I really haven't understood what you meant. What was written in that contract or deed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any of the contracts. It's only what I heard. I heard when Sibincic said what he said, what they were supposed to do, at a citizens' rally to a little group of refugees. He told them, "Do such and such. Make up a false contract. When the police comes, they won't do anything to you. You're legally here." But I didn't actually see a contract myself. It's only something I heard about. And how the police acted, that the police acted only when the real owner came in from abroad and put into motion legal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... understand me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood well, they were Serbs coming from Croatia who would receive or would be given houses. However, the Croat owners of those houses did not consent freely to this takeover of their houses. Is it what happened?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't the property, it was a contract saying that they agreed with the owner that he was giving his property over for temporary use by these other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have some knowledge in this area, due to my former occupation or former job. I think the situation you're describing is very simple. Mr. Sibincic told the refugees that they should draw fake contracts so that they have a deed that would entitle them to occupy houses, and that's what the refugees did. Somebody gave them fake contracts with fake signatures. They signed, and that was it. But the real owners are not aware of what's going on, because they're probably abroad. They may be working in Germany, in Milan, elsewhere. And when they come back, they find out that their houses are being occupied by Serbs. At that stage, they go immediately to the police station to say, "Look, what's going on? Somebody is in our house." Then the police come, and then the whole situation is discovered. Is it what happened?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this is a good summary of what was happening at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSA EJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So I think it's clear for everybody now. Mr. Ferrara, would you like time to redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't have any redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on behalf of the Judges of this Chamber, I would like to thank you for coming to The Hague at the request of the Prosecution, to give a statement on the events which took place in your village. Thank you for coming. Thank you for testifying, and I wish you well and I wish you a safe trip back to your country. I would like Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, and with your permission I have unloaded a great burden -- lifted a great burden off my shoulders during my stay here. Goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis or Mr. Ferrara, as far as next week is concerned -- yes, yes, I was about to forget. The number, yes. We've discussed the issue, and we'll have a final exhibit number. Thank you for reminding us. Mr. Registrar, you remember that an exhibit was an MFI number, this article from the Chicago newspaper needs a final number, so what is it going to be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be -- the MFI number initially was P559. It will now be Exhibit P559.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Now, as regards next week, I'm not going to give any name - you never know - but we have VS-1133 scheduled for next week. According to the table provided by the Prosecution, we'll need three days for that witness. There's also a VS-1134, another witness. It will be a 92 ter witness. Am I right, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. There are no other changes or additional information concerning next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards 1133, how much time will you need? Experience has shown that two hours or three hours means almost three days, so how much do you need for 1133? I'm talking about the examination-in-chief. Unfortunately, I don't have the document before me, so maybe you don't have it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe the witness was listed down as 2.5 hours or -- 2 or 2.5 hours. My colleague, who will be leading him in court, will not be finishing the proofing until Monday, so it's a bit premature to give a more revised estimate. But we have him down, 1133, down for Tuesday, Wednesday, and continuing into Thursday if need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, and then we'll hear 1134, a 92 ter witness. If Mr. Seselj doesn't wish to cross-examine him, he won't. This is his absolute right, of course, and there won't be any problem. We know what is the position of the parties on this. Thank you. Very well. Mr. Seselj, an administrative matter you wish to raise with the Court?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, just with respect to the next witness or, rather, the next two witnesses. I read both statements which The Hague Prosecutors had these witnesses give, and I'm convinced that no examination-in-chief will last longer than one to one and a half hours, because there's nothing much, in my opinion, that they can ask. So both of them can be heard viva voce, and an hour and a half be accorded to each of them, if there is the goodwill for that. If there's something else, well, then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We've noted what you've just said. Mr. Seselj, you mentioned it several times, and Judge Harhoff, my colleague, also reminded you of this, and there should be no misunderstanding among the public about the measures that are being applied to you. The Registrar has decided to wire-tap your conversations. It is true. It has been done according to the Rules. I told you what my opinion about this was, but that's the way it is. Your phone is tapped. It means that you can use your phone, you can use your phone and call your associates. There is no question about it. Of course you can call them. If you don't want to, of course, that's up to you to decide. I think my colleague would like to say something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. President. You see, Mr. Seselj, we have discussed this at several reprisals, and the issue, as far as I have understood it, is that as long as your collaborators in Belgrade are unwilling to provide the information to the Registrar that the Registrar has asked, as long will your communication with your group in Belgrade remain supervised. Now, if you are in control of your associates in Belgrade, all it takes is for you to instruct them to provide to the Registrar the information that the Registrar has asked for, and the matter will be solved. So as long as you do nothing, this situation will remain, and therefore I have a difficulty in accepting that you are suffering prejudice, because you, yourself, are in control of these matters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, my legal advisers have answered all the questions put by the Registrar. The fact that the Registrar is not satisfied with their answers is the Registrar's problem, and they're not going to respond any more. Secondly, I have to have sensitive conversations and discussions with my associates, not to be tapped in to, because we have to assess whether we're going to deal with a fact during a cross-examination or not. And then the material that I receive from them by fax, I have to see whether some of it is useful and what is and what isn't, to make a selection, and not have the Registrar select my material and to inform the Prosecutor what it was that I discussed and which papers I received. So because of that, I don't want to discuss the trial with them at all, and when I talk to them, I ask them what the public thinks, having looked at the television footage and what the media says. So I'm the one that is in control of my Defence case and that is my right, so I will not allow anybody to tap into my telephone conversations with my legal advisers. If somebody does that, then I'm not going to have those conversations. And once again, in that way, in that fashion, stop them from tapping in to my conversations. That's the only thing I can do, to stop having conversations, and then they have nothing to tap into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I accept the fact that you need to prepare your Defence case in a privileged environment. However, I cannot accept for you to say that the Registrar will give the documents you might receive to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I heard you say that too. You think that when a document is received by the Registrar, and the Registrar goes straight to the Prosecutor to give him a copy of that document? I find it hard to believe, because if it was the case, it would be very serious and he could end up in jail. So I find it hard to believe. That's what you think, that's what you think, but I find it hard to believe. If you have evidence of this, then show it to us. But somebody sends you a document, the registrar -- not the Court Registrar but somebody else from within the Registry will go to the Prosecutor and say, "Look, Mr. Seselj has received this document, please take a look," when the Judges don't even know about this? I find it really hard to believe. It would be a major surprise for me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, a few days ago I provided you with some important and valuable information. The former deputy of -- Deputy Secretary David Tolbert two or three years ago became the Deputy of the Prosecutor-in-Chief, Carla Del Ponte. Now I have the latest, freshest information. I learned from a reliable source, and you can check this out with David Tolbert, that about two years ago David Tolbert had meetings with Tomislav Nikolic to discuss me and my trial. So check that out, please, Mr. President. Ask David Tolbert to tell you whether he indeed did have meetings with Tomislav Nikolic or not and what the reasons for those meetings were. There's a plot against me here. The Registrar has been dealing me a bad deal for all these years, much more than the Prosecutor. They have prohibited me from having telephone conversations with even my closest family and visits from my closest family, and the reason they said was that my party had received a large number of votes at the last elections and to prevent me from taking part in forming the next Serbian government. That was the official reason provided on the letterhead of the Registry, so I have no reason to try and convince you of this, that the secretariat is in cohorts and plotting with goodness knows who else against me, but please check that fact out, whether David Tolbert did have a meeting about two years ago with Tomislav Nikolic in order to discuss the trial against me. If you check that out, everything will become clear to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, this is a tangent. The issue was whether you could resolve yourself the problem of supervision of your communication with your Defence. Team in Belgrade. The Registrar has asked a question to them, and they have not given a satisfactory answer. The question, if you want to know, that was put to your collaborators in Belgrade was whether any of them had or had not participated in conference calls between you and other persons who were not privileged by way of the privileged telephone line between the 4th of January, 2007, and the 10th of September, 2008. That's a simple question, and this has not been answered by your collaborators. And if you instruct them to provide the simple answer, "yes" or "no," then the situation is resolved. That's all it takes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Harhoff, I answered that question. I gave the Registry the answer in a handwritten submission, and I said that my telephone conversations, privileged telephone conversations with legal advisers, were attended by members of my Defence team. My Defence team consists of a team of legal advisers. In addition to the three registered, I have several other lawyers working on my case and a team of investigators too. Depending on what was on the agenda here in court, certain investigators attended the conversation. And I confirm that in addition to the legal advisers, there was some other people who joined in the consultations, but I insist upon the fact that it was only members of the team for my Defence who took part, and the composition of that team is something that I let the Registry know in advance on time. So how can I defend myself without contacting my investigators? How could I have instructed the investigators to compile (redacted) was uncovered and unveiled? That is the fruit of their labour, pursuant to my instructions. They are my extended arm in all this. So you can assess the success of my cross-examination and the valuable work of my advisers, not only my legal advisers but my investigators as well, because you can see that there is no secret for us, no problem that cannot be resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, in order to be clear, the problem flows from two different things, and I'm going to explain what they are, and I'll go slowly so that everybody can understand, because it's a very complicated issue for people who did not follow the whole process. You were granted the right to self-defense. It means that you must have the necessary means to investigate, because of course the Defence has to carry out its own investigation to prepare for cross-examination and to prepare its own case. In my mind, since I issued a decision on the necessary financial means to support your Defence case, in my mind you had the right to have contacts with the person assisting you in your case. That was the legal position. On top of this, another element came into play, and these are, namely, the inherent powers of the Registrar. Since your associates had to have access to the Detention Centre and may have received some kind of remuneration, the Registrar, on its own initiative, without consulting with the Pre-Trial Judge, i.e., me at the time, the Registrar decided that there would be a privilege agreement within the Registrar system. The situation is now as follows: There is some kind of a clash between the administrative system, the Registrar administrative system, and the rights of Defence, and this is an important issue. There are various possibilities to solve the problems. The first one is you could have challenged the decision by referring it to the President, according with the rules of detention, which gives you that right. You could have filed a motion, referred to the Chamber. We could have issued a decision on this motion. Then you could have appealed the decision. This is an example of a solution that could have been found, and that's where we stand at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me remind you that the President of this Tribunal acts in two capacities; as a legal person and the President of the Court, presiding over the Appeals Chamber, so as the judiciary, and in the administrative sense, in this case as the second-instance organ in relation to the Registry. I categorically state that no administrative organ has the right to clip the right to my Defence, neither the Registry nor the President of the Tribunal. And with respect to my elementary right to a defence, I don't want to discuss that with them. I appealed to the President of the Tribunal because they seized 250 Euros and two diskettes that the Prosecution had provided me with, so I did complain because of that. That was an administrative issue. The right to my Defence cannot be an administrative issue, and so I address you orally as the Trial Chamber. In my legal system, the legal system of Serbia, orally addressing the Court has the same weight as a written submission, and I suppose that that is the same in the civilised world. What I say in court and is recorded and becomes a record of the proceedings is the same as a written submission; perhaps less detailed, but nonetheless carrying the same weight. So I have addressed you on that issue. Now, if you have the right to resolve the problem in exercising your duties, then I expect you to do so. If you have not been given that possibility and can't resolve the problem, then the problem remains unsolved until the end, and I continue to defend myself alone. I am alone in the universe, in the cosmos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, okay, I think the whole issue has been clarified. I understand now you're referring this matter to the Chamber, orally. Since it is quite a complex issue, maybe you should submit written submissions. But, of course, it is your right to make an oral submission. I won't challenge the logic here, but of course the Prosecution, who is also interested in this matter, can also submit oral submissions or written submissions on this simple question, can the Registrar obstruct the rights of Defence by tapping telephone conversations and by receiving documents that are received by an accused from his team, and the other way around?" I think it's a simple matter, a simple question. Maybe the answer will be much more complicated. Mr. Mundis, what's your intention? Would you like to submit written submissions or maybe to provide an oral answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I'm very quickly looking at the rules of detention, and it's, I believe, relatively clear that the appeal of this decision has to go to the President of the Tribunal. And so our position would be that the only thing that the Trial Chamber could do would be to refer any submissions by the accused directly to the President for his decision and determination. Until such a point in time as that happens, it's premature to be putting any position onto the record. Of course, I would imagine in those circumstances the Registrar very well may be desirous of being heard on the point, since it was his decision under the various regulations that apply. So at this point in time, our view would be that the rules of detention are very clear. It's a matter for the President to decide, and that the Trial Chamber has no authority to act on this matter, other than, of course, to refer the appeal by the accused to the President for his determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should the Trial Chamber feel that it has competence, what would be the position of the Prosecutor? Would you make written submissions or oral submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I mean, I think our position with respect to the conduct of the accused and his associates has been made very clear. In the event that the accused makes further written submissions, we will certainly address the issue to the Trial Chamber, or perhaps if the Chamber does, in fact, refer it to the President, we very well may seek to provide some written submissions on that point directly to the President. I don't really have anything else to add on this point at this time. Again, we've, in a number of different filings and orally, have made our position quite clear. Of course, our view is that this entire situation has arisen as a direct result of the misconduct of the accused and his associates, and that's clearly our position, and he has no, as we would say, no clean hands to complain about the Registrar's decision, since it was based upon factual findings concerning the misconduct of the accused and his associates. I don't know if that's the end of that discussion, Mr. President. I do have a couple of other issues that need to be raised before we adjourn, and I am also looking at the clock. Perhaps we might need to take a break and then resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we have enough time. Mr. Seselj has been heard. You can raise your two issues, and then we can suspend. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had one thing to say first, and now I have two things. With respect to the clean hands/dirty hands, I think that the dirtiest hands are those which are in the indictment and inscribed there, saying that at the rally in Hrtkovci, I strove for children of mixed marriages to be killed, so so much about clean hands and dirty hands. Now I have to object to what the Prosecution says, that it's not up to the Trial Chamber to resolve this problem. I think that it is only the Trial Chamber that is in a position to resolve this problem, because they are the only guarantor of the justness and fairness of the proceedings and the only guarantor of the right to present my Defence and ensure a fair trial. The Trial Chamber is the one who is there to protect my rights from anybody jeopardising them. They can be jeopardised by the Registrar, by the President of the Tribunal, by the prison guards, by anybody, and it is up to the Trial Chamber to protect my rights to a proper Defence. And that Defence and my rights cannot be jeopardised in any way, because if they are, there can be no fair and just trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The two other topics, very quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. On the 23rd of September, my colleague Ms. Dahl indicated to the Trial Chamber that we would be filing a Rule 77 application with respect to the publication of the (redacted) Earlier, just a few moments ago, as reflected on page 82 and into page 83, Dr. Seselj made some statements which, in light of our stated intention to file that application, very well might be considered to be incriminatory, and we would ask that the Trial Chamber at this point perhaps caution Mr. Seselj with respect to statements that he might make concerning that book, and how that book was produced, and who produced that book under his direction, because to be as transparent as possible, the statements that he has made concerning this book very well might be considered incriminatory in the context of a Rule 77 application, which should be filed later today but which we've orally indicated from the 23rd of September would be forthcoming. And so we believe that he should be cautioned that anything that he states on the record concerning that book very well might form the basis of further action in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know this book. I don't know what's in the book. We're totally in the dark right now. Let's wait and -- wait for your submissions. Second point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, again, just for the record, it's our view that the accused should be cautioned concerning statements that he might make concerning this book, and the authorship of it, and who was working on it and under whose supervision. The final point for today, Mr. President, concerns the expert Ms. Ewa Tabeau, and my colleague, Ms. Biersay, would like to briefly address Your Honours on that expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I don't know this book, I don't know what's in the book. Mr. Mundis said very important things. You've heard him well. We're not going to start debating this, because the Judges can't really debate -- start debating on something that they have no knowledge of. Mr. Mundis said what he had to say. It's on the transcript. You know exactly what he meant. Mrs. Biersay, we haven't seen you for a long time. I'm very glad to see you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am here to quickly give you a status report with respect to Madam Tabeau. Today, we'll be giving a letter to the accused, to whom we have already disclosed her testimony from seven trials, and we have two remaining trials to transcribe, and we're hoping to have those completed by Tuesday. So I wanted to make the Court aware of that. And a second issue is: We have also previously provided to Mr. Seselj approximately nine reports, previous reports of Madam Tabeau, and we are going to give him a list of some others so that he can choose which ones, if any, he would like to have. We were concerned about giving him all these reports that may not, in his eyes, be relevant, so we are submitting this letter to him so that he can tell us whether he wants all of them, or none of them, or some of them. So I just wanted to give the Court that report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I demand that all the reports be submitted to me, and I'm counting on the kindness of the OTP that now they are going to send, once again, what it was that they sent me earlier on so, so that I don't go through the trouble of going through all the documents that got all messed up by the prison guards during this summer. Why am I asking for this? Because I'm going to challenge the credibility of Ewa Tabeau, and especially in respect of the report on Srebrenica, with the thesis that she is taking part in the falsification of the actual event that took place there, and I'm telling you that openly. That's why I need all of this, and I'm totally going to challenge her credibility and her expert knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Challenge, but challenge quickly, please. Ms. Tabeau is scheduled for two weeks from now, I think, in a fortnight. The Trial Chamber will first make a decision to see whether this will be a viva voce testimony or whether it will be a cross-examination by Defence with no in-chief and with only the reports being tendered. But we need to know exactly what you intend to do quickly, Mr. Seselj. We need to know what you're challenging, which points you're challenging. You stated mentioning Srebrenica. I mean, we have not been seized of Srebrenica, and this Trial Chamber is not involved in this matter. So we are waiting for your submissions, your written submissions. I believe it's time to adjourn. We're running out of tape. We will resume next week, in the afternoon. So we will meet again on Tuesday at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of October, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25
